ev.f_miracle.text.1: A neighbour who had not left her bed for years suddenly walked again after someone brought her water from a holy spring. The whole quarter is buzzing, and people are already streaming to the spring.
ev.f_miracle.text.2: The old beggar who had sat asking for alms at the gate for ten years washed his face with dew from a stone on the hill – and, they say, saw his own hands. Now people climb to that stone from dawn to dusk.
ev.f_miracle.go.2: Climb to the stone on the hill
ev.f_miracle.text.3: The dead tree by the road – the old folk say a holy man once prayed beneath it – has burst into blossom out of season. People tie scraps of cloth to its branches and whisper their requests.
ev.f_miracle.go.3: Go to the tree with a request of your own
ev.f_miracle.tell.3: Tell the whole market about the miracle
ev.f_miracle.text.4: Herdsmen found a spring in a cave beyond the village where no spring had ever been. The first to drink from it was a lame herdsman – and he came back down without leaning on his stick.
ev.f_miracle.go.4: Make your way to the cave
ev.f_miracle.tell.4: Spread the word through the district
ev.f_miracle.text.5: Three nights running a pale, steady light hung over the old shrine on the hill. The keeper swears he lit no fire, and a man sick with fever who slept there woke up well.
ev.f_miracle.go.5: Spend a night at the shrine
ev.f_miracle.text.6: The water-carrier's mute boy, whom everyone took for simple, drank from the well by an old holy man's tomb and suddenly said, “I'm thirsty.” Now the well is guarded and its water sold by the sip.
ev.f_miracle.go.6: Buy a sip from the well
ev.f_miracle.tell.6: Retell the story to everyone you know
ev.f_miracle.text.7: A hermit has settled in a hut beyond the hills. They say he laid his palm on the head of a child who had shaken with fever for a week – and the fever left. A trail of petitioners leads to his hut, each carrying at least a flatbread.
ev.f_miracle.go.7: Go to the hermit with an offering
ev.f_miracle.text.8: The drought has scorched everything, yet one morning the old dry well at the edge of the village was full to the brim. The water is cold and sweet, and everyone who drank swears they feel stronger.
ev.f_miracle.go.8: Go and draw water at the well
ev.f_miracle.tell.8: Spread the news to the nearby villages
ev.f_miracle.text.9: A farmer dug up a stone that seems to bear the print of a hand. That same year his back, which had ached for twenty years, stopped hurting – and now people bring gifts to the stone from all around.
ev.f_miracle.go.9: Bring a gift to the stone
ev.f_miracle.text.10: An old neighbour dreamed three times of a spot by the river where they should dig. The whole yard dug – and found a cold spring. A weaver who was going blind washed her eyes in it first, and can see the thread again.
ev.f_miracle.text.11: A fire burned down the whole street, yet the little shrine in the middle of it stood untouched – not even the cloth ribbons on it were scorched. The burned-out families sleep by its walls and say there's no fear or pain there.
ev.f_miracle.go.11: Go and pray at the shrine
ev.f_miracle.text.12: A lame potter lay in the black mud by a hot spring beyond the hills – and came back on foot, though he had left on a stretcher. Everyone with an ache is heading there, and a flatbread seller has already set up by the spring.
ev.f_miracle.text.13: A ragged wanderer passed through the village and blessed the well – and the water, bitter for years, ran clear, and everyone who drank was cured of their stomach troubles. The wanderer is gone, but now people pray at the well every morning.
ev.f_miracle.text.14: A deaf old woman from the next street spent a night on the mountain by the holy place, and in the morning came down asking who was singing so loudly. It was the birds. Now a whole line of people is climbing up.
ev.f_miracle.tell.14: Tell everyone about the old woman
ev.f_miracle.text.15: A shepherd boy went missing in the hills and was found five days later – alive, fed and calm. He says a “lady in white” fed him by a stream under three trees. Now people go to the three trees with offerings.
ev.f_miracle.tell.15: Retell the story on every corner
ev.f_miracle.text.16: On a feast day a cripple with a withered arm dipped into the river at the holy ford – and came out clenching and unclenching his fingers. The crowd gasped, and by morning you couldn't get near the ford.
ev.a_eclipse.text.1: In broad daylight the sun went dark, as if someone had cupped a hand over it. Dogs howled, old women wailed, then the light came back – and everyone pretended they hadn't been frightened at all.
ev.a_eclipse.text.2: In the middle of the market it suddenly grew dark: the sun shrank to a thin sickle. Traders abandoned their stalls, some prayed, some made off with other people's fruit – and you never worked out which was more frightening.
ev.a_eclipse.text.3: That night the moon turned a deep red, as if it had been dipped in blood. The old people said it boded ill, and nobody for miles around slept a wink until morning.
ev.a_eclipse.text.4: You were on the road when a shadow crept over the sun and it suddenly turned cold as dusk. The birds fell silent all at once. When the light came back you noticed you had been gripping your staff like a weapon the whole time.
ev.a_eclipse.text.5: The sun went out in the middle of someone's wedding. The guests decided it was a bad omen, the groom that it was a good one, and the bride burst into tears. When the light returned, everyone acted as though it had all been planned.
ev.a_eclipse.text.6: The stargazer had predicted back in spring that the sun would darken, and people laughed at him. It darkened at exactly the hour he named. Now the laughter is quieter, and there's a crowd outside the stargazer's house.
ev.a_eclipse.text.7: When the shadow crept across the sun, the whole street poured outside and banged on pots and bowls to drive off whatever was devouring it. You banged loudest of all. The sun came back – so it worked.
ev.a_eclipse.text.8: In the night the moon began to melt away at the edge until only a dull copper disc was left. Dogs howled, neighbours prayed on the rooftops, and you sat on the doorstep unable to look away.
ev.a_eclipse.text.9: At noon the stars came out. You saw them with your own eyes – in daylight! – and for a long time afterwards you told everyone who would listen, and plenty who wouldn't.
ev.a_eclipse.text.10: The day before, the keepers of the shrine told everyone to pray and fast: the sky, they said, would show a sign. The sign came – the sun went black for a while. You prayed harder than you had in years.
ev.a_eclipse.text.11: The light turned strange, a greyish yellow, and the shadows grew sharp as knives. The patches of light under a tree became hundreds of tiny sickles. You stared at them until the sun was whole again.
ev.a_eclipse.text.12: The sun dimmed, and by evening the whole town knew it foretold the death of someone great. They argued only over who. Just in case, you set an extra lamp by your door.
ev.a_eclipse.text.13: Darkness fell so fast that the neighbours' little ones shrieked and crammed themselves under the awning, and you followed them – trying not to run. It was soon over, but for a week the children teased you for a scaredy-cat.
ev.a_eclipse.text.14: You were drawing water when the water in your jar suddenly went black – the sky reflected in it had darkened. Looking up, you saw the sun with a bite taken out of it and nearly dropped the jar.
ev.a_eclipse.text.15: The festival was in full swing when the sun began to go out. The music broke off, the food went cold, and everyone stared upward in silence. When the light came back, nobody dared carry on celebrating.
ev.a_eclipse.text.16: The old woman next door looked at the blackened sun and calmly said she'd seen this as a girl – and they'd all lived. You wanted to believe her, but you kept close to the door all the same.
ev.f_vow.text.1: On that terrible night when the storm nearly tore the house down, you swore that if you survived you would bring a rich gift to the temple. The storm passed. It's time to pay.
ev.f_vow.text.1.islamic: On that terrible night when the storm nearly tore the house down, you swore to God that if you survived you would feed forty poor people. The storm passed. It's time to keep your vow.
ev.f_vow.text.1.jewish: On that terrible night when the storm nearly tore the house down, you swore that if you survived you would give generously to the synagogue and the poor. The storm passed. It's time to keep your vow.
ev.f_vow.text.2: When the fever had been shaking you for three weeks, you promised: if you got back on your feet, you would give a generous gift to a holy cause. You're up. Your legs still tremble, but the promise is already waiting.
ev.f_vow.text.3: The flood caught the raft at the crossing, and clinging to a log you swore to feed a hundred poor people if you got out. The current threw you onto a sandbank. A hundred poor people won't feed themselves.
ev.f_vow.text.4: When the neighbours' roof was burning and sparks were landing on yours, you promised heaven a generous gift if only the wind would turn. The wind turned. The neighbours still talk about the miracle – and ask what you promised.
ev.f_vow.text.5: Bandits stepped out at you in the hills, and standing with your hands raised you swore that if you lived you would give generously to a holy place. The bandits took only your cloak and left. You miss the cloak, but the vow remains.
ev.f_vow.text.6: The drought had dragged into its second month, and you promised to give a good share of what you own to the needy if rain came. Yesterday it poured. The earth is drinking, and you are counting what the promise will cost.
ev.f_vow.text.7: When the plague was moving through the district and someone was carried out every day, you swore that if the sickness passed your house by, you would give a rich gift to a shrine. The plague has gone, and it never touched your house. Now it's your turn.
ev.f_vow.text.8: You put everything you had into one venture, and on a sleepless night you promised that if it worked out you'd give a generous share to the poor and to a holy place. It worked out. Somehow that share now seems far too generous.
ev.f_vow.text.9: The path crumbled under your feet, and hanging over the drop by a tree root you swore that if you got out you would bring a rich gift. A passing traveller pulled you up. You thanked the traveller. Heaven you haven't thanked yet.
ev.f_vow.text.10: In the night the ground shook, clay rained from the walls, and pressed flat to the floor you promised that if the house stood you would give a generous gift to a holy cause. The house stood, with just a crack across one wall. The crack reminds you of the vow every morning.
ev.f_vow.text.11: You were accused of something you didn't do, and on the eve of the trial you swore that if you were cleared you would give generously to the poor. The accuser tangled himself up in his own lies, and you were let go. The poor don't know about it yet. But you do.
ev.f_vow.text.12: When your old friend lay in a fever and the healer was already spreading his hands, you promised a generous gift to a holy place in exchange for his life. Your friend pulled through and is already grumbling about the food. But you were the one who made the promise.
ev.f_vow.title.13: A Vow for What Was Lost
ev.f_vow.text.13: You lost the bundle holding all your savings and in despair promised that if it turned up you'd give half to a holy cause. It turned up in a ditch right by your house. Half isn't all of it, is it?
ev.f_vow.text.14: When the enemy stood beneath the walls and burning arrows flew over the rooftops at night, you swore to give a rich gift to a shrine if the town held. The enemy left as suddenly as it came. The town is celebrating, and it's time for you to keep your word.
ev.f_vow.text.15: A snake bit you in the tall grass, and as your leg grew heavy you whispered a promise: if you lived, you'd feed every beggar at the holy place. You lived. The beggars at the holy place, it seems, have already heard.
ev.f_vow.text.16: Many years ago, in a year of hunger, you promised that if you lived to see better days you'd share generously with those worse off. The better days came, and today you saw a hungry old man at your door – and remembered it all, word for word.
ev.marriage_m.text.1: Your relatives think it's time you had a family. There is a bride with a good dowry, but your heart is elsewhere.
ev.marriage_m.text.2: The matchmaker has called three times with the same story: a rich bride, her dowry a chest and half a field. Meanwhile, for three months you've been carrying water past the house where a quite different girl lives – and not because it's the shorter way.
ev.marriage_m.text.3: A wealthy trader hints that he wouldn't mind a family tie: his niece comes with a shop and all its stock. You nodded and tallied the gain – and in the evening went down to the river again, where the girl from the next street rinses linen and laughs at you.
ev.marriage_m.text.4: At every festival the aunties whisper that you've stayed a bachelor too long. They like a bride from a good house – modest and with a dowry. You like another: the one who out-danced everyone at that same festival.
ev.marriage_m.text.5: They're matching you with a young widow: a solid house, a working household and not a single debt. But you keep thinking of the girl you exchanged a few words with at the well – she has nothing but her laugh and her stubborn eyes.
ev.marriage_m.text.6: They say that when you were still a boy, the elders agreed to marry you to a girl from a well-off family. The girl has grown up, and her dowry with her. Only your heart has long been taken – and not by her.
ev.marriage_m.text.7: The family has gathered round the table and is briskly listing it all: this bride brings land, that one a link to important people. You sit in silence, thinking of a third – one best not mentioned at this table.
ev.marriage_m.text.8: A well-placed neighbour offers to match you with his ward – with a dowry you never dreamed of. Refusing such a man is not easy. And the girl you really do dream of, he has never even laid eyes on.
ev.marriage_m.text.9: At the bride-viewing the girl sat with lowered eyes while her family talked of chests, cloth and land. You listened with half an ear: in the doorway stood a serving girl with a jug, barely holding back her laughter – just like you.
ev.marriage_m.text.10: Your friends have long been married and say as one: take the one with the dowry, love comes later. Maybe so. But the other one pressed a flower into your hand yesterday and ran off, and you haven't been thinking straight since.
ev.marriage_m.text.11: The whole street already knows you're being matched with a rich bride – they knew before you did. Only one girl on that same street has stopped saying hello to you. And somehow that's what keeps you awake.
ev.marriage_m.text.12: They're offering a bride who comes with enough to pay off every debt and have plenty left. You honestly try to be glad. But all you can see is the girl who mended nets by the river and never once asked how much you own.
ev.marriage_m.text.13: After the harvest festival, matchmakers came from a wealthy household: the matter, they say, is settled, it only needs your word. You do have a word to give. Only it's already promised – in a whisper, to the girl who waited for you by the old tree after the festival.
ev.marriage_m.text.14: The elders say a man your age shouldn't live alone, and they've already picked out a bride with a dowry. A good girl, everyone praises her. But more and more often you linger by the house where another one lives.
ev.marriage_m.text.15: The bride with the dowry means a roof over your head, well-fed years and the neighbours' respect. The bride of your heart means – you don't quite know what, but just thinking of her makes you grin like a fool. The family is waiting for an answer.
ev.marriage_m.text.16: Word has come from a neighbouring settlement: there's a bride there with a fine dowry, and her family is willing. It's two days' journey. And the one you think about every night lives two doors away.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.1: Your neighbor demands compensation: your animals, he says, trampled his vegetable garden. He has two witnesses, both of them his cousins.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.1.athens: Your neighbor has filed suit: your donkey, he says, trampled his vegetable garden. Hundreds of citizen jurors will decide, and they favor whoever speaks more beautifully.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.1.egypt: Your neighbor has petitioned the strategos: your donkey, he says, trampled his vegetable garden. The official demands that you answer, and both the neighbor's witnesses are his cousins.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.1.rome: Your neighbor demands compensation: your donkey, he says, trampled his vegetable garden. He summoned you before the praetor right in the middle of the street, in front of everyone, and both his witnesses are his cousins.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.2: Your neighbour claims you owe him for a sack of grain borrowed last spring. You remember perfectly well that you returned it – but he has two witnesses, and you only have your memory.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.2: You reminded everyone that on the day you returned the grain, the neighbour's witnesses had helped you carry it themselves. The witnesses looked at each other and fell silent.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.3: Your neighbour wants compensation for his fence: he says you knocked it flat while turning round with a load of brushwood. The fence is indeed lying on the ground. But in your view it's lying there from old age, and the neighbour's witnesses think otherwise.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.3: You brought a piece of that very fence to court. It crumbled to dust right in the judge's hands.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.4: Your neighbour complains that you diverted water from the shared ditch onto your plot and his beds dried out. His witnesses – his own hired hands – say they saw you “poking about at the dam at night.”
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.4: You asked how, on a moonless night, anyone could make out from the far end of the field who was digging at the dam. The neighbour's workers immediately started arguing about who had seen what.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.5: Your neighbour at the market demands compensation: your awning, he says, leaked in the rain right onto his cloth. He waves a wet bolt at the judge while two traders from his row nod at every word.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.5: You pointed out that the bolt was wet only along one edge – the one that had been lying on the ground. The judge felt the cloth and snorted.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.6: Your neighbour demands half the fruit from your tree: the branches hang over his yard, he says, so half the crop is his. His witnesses are ready to confirm that the tree's shadow falls on his roof.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.6: You offered the neighbour half of the fallen leaves you rake up every year as well. The judges laughed, and the neighbour gave up.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.7: Your neighbour's shed burned down, and he is sure the sparks came from your hearth. Two witnesses swear smoke was pouring from your house that night. He demands you pay for the shed and everything in it.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.7: You reminded the court that you'd spent that night in the next village, and half the village is ready to vouch for it. A hearth doesn't light itself.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.8: Your neighbour has lodged a complaint: he says you called him a thief in front of everyone and blackened his good name. You did say something – in a temper, at the well. The witnesses remembered every word and even added a few.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.8: You asked the witnesses to repeat your words – and each repeated them differently. By the third telling, “crook” had turned into “crow.”
ev.a_lawsuit.text.9: Your neighbour demands compensation: your bees, he says, stung his hired man so badly he couldn't go out to the field for a week. The witnesses show off swollen hands and swear the bees came from your yard.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.9: You asked how the witnesses could tell your bees from anyone else's. One honestly answered, “By their spite.” Everyone roared with laughter.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.10: Your neighbour insists he lent you a good axe and you returned it chipped. Now he wants a new one – and he's brought along two witnesses who saw what the axe looked like before.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.10: You asked the witnesses to describe the axe. One said it had a long handle, the other a short one, and both turned to look at the neighbour.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.11: The shared wall between your yards collapsed after the rains, and your neighbour demands that you repair it: he says you were digging a cellar under it. Two witnesses “heard you digging.”
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.11: You invited the judges to inspect your cellar. There turned out to be no cellar at all – just a heap of old pots. The neighbour turned purple.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.12: Your neighbour demands compensation: in the middle of the harvest his hired man abandoned his field and came to work for you – so you must have lured him away. Witnesses heard you “praising your soup.”
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.12: You called the hired man himself. He said he hadn't left for the soup but to get away from the neighbour's shouting, and pointed at the neighbour. Even the judges couldn't help smiling.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.13: Your neighbour wants compensation for a fouled well: he says you tipped slops into it. Two witnesses from his household swear they saw you at the well at dawn with a bucket.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.13: You showed the judges that the neighbour's well sits behind locked gates and only he has the key. The witnesses suddenly recalled that it had been rather dark.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.14: Your neighbour demands payment for torn clothes and his fright: your dog, he says, went for him right at the gate. Witnesses saw him running, and the dog still barks at the mere mention of his name.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.14: You brought the dog to court. The old hound lay down at the judge's feet, yawned and fell asleep. The case was closed amid general laughter.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.15: Your neighbour has remembered that years ago you supposedly promised him part of your harvest for helping you build. He remembers every word, and his two friends remember even better.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.15: You asked the neighbour's friends what year it had been. One named the year of the drought, the other the year of the flood. The judges exchanged looks.
ev.a_lawsuit.text.16: Your neighbour demands compensation for a big jar of oil: he says you brushed against it in passing and it cracked. His witnesses – his lodgers – say they heard a clink and your voice.
ev.a_lawsuit.self.success.16: You pointed out that the crack in the jar had long since gone black with oil and grime. “It must have clinked about five years ago,” you said, and the judges laughed.
ev.y_scolding.text.3: {npc}, your mother, found a frog in her basket of yarn. It wasn't hard to work out whose frog it was: you were the only one in the house who knew its name.
ev.y_scolding.text.4: {npc}, your mother, sent you for water in the morning. You came back at sunset – with an empty jar, soaked to the ears and with a story about a fish the size of a dog. The story didn't help.
ev.y_scolding.text.5: You decided to help by sweeping the yard – straight into the hearth, embers and all. {npc}, your mother, spent a long time chasing the smoke out of the house and even longer explaining where helping ends.
ev.y_scolding.text.6: {npc}, your mother, spent three days searching for her best comb. It turned up under your bedding: you had been combing the puppy with it.
ev.y_scolding.text.7: You drew all the neighbours in charcoal on the freshly whitewashed wall – very lifelike, especially the fat trader. {npc}, your mother, admired the likeness but made you scrub the wall clean.
ev.y_scolding.text.8: {npc}, your mother, caught you on the roof: you were planning to see whether you could fly if you flapped hard enough. You didn't learn to fly, but you did have to sit through a long speech.
ev.y_scolding.text.9: You traded your new shirt for a clay whistle from the boy next door. {npc}, your mother, listened to what a good deal you'd made and sent you straight back to trade it back.
ev.y_scolding.text.10: {npc}, your mother, set the dough out in the sun to rise, and you made little people out of it to play with. The little people came out wonderfully. There was no bread that day.
ev.y_scolding.text.11: You got into a fight with the neighbours' kids and came home with a torn sleeve, a skinned knee and a very pleased look. {npc}, your mother, was not pleased.
ev.y_scolding.text.12: {npc}, your mother, told you to keep an eye on the porridge on the fire. And you did keep an eye – on a beetle crawling up the wall. The porridge kept an eye on itself and burned.
ev.y_scolding.text.13: You hid in the laundry basket and stayed there half the day while the whole yard searched for you. {npc}, your mother, was the last to find you – and the first to tell you what she thought of you.
ev.y_scolding.text.14: {npc}, your mother, sent you to the neighbour for a pinch of salt. You came back half a day later – without the salt but with news about the whole street. {npc} listened to the news, and then it was your turn to listen.
ev.y_scolding.text.15: You decided to wash your shirt yourself – in the jar of drinking water. {npc}, your mother, appreciated your independence, but the water had to be fetched all over again. And you were the one who fetched it.
ev.y_scolding.text.16: You told the guests that {npc}, your mother, calls them “old gossips” behind their backs. It was the plain truth – and that's exactly why a long talk awaited you that evening.
ev.v_rage_home.text.1: It had been a bad day, and at home some small thing set you off – spilled soup. You slammed your fist on the table so hard the bowls flew to the floor, and the household froze.
ev.v_rage_home.text.2: All day long people had cheated you and hurried you, and at home someone picked the wrong moment to ask where the promised money was. You shouted so loud a pot fell off the shelf, and the whole house went silent at once.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.2: You gathered up the pieces of the pot and quietly told them what kind of day it had been. They heard you out – not at once, but they did.
ev.v_rage_home.text.3: You came home to find the hearth had gone out and no one had fetched water. One word led to another – and you slammed the door so hard the frame cracked. The house went as quiet as before a storm.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.3: You rekindled the hearth yourself, fetched the water, and only then asked forgiveness. It worked better than any words.
ev.v_rage_home.text.4: Someone in the household took your favourite cup without asking and dropped it. You snatched up the shards, flung them at the wall and went on shouting for ages that nothing could be left alone in this house.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.4: You admitted the cup mattered less than the frightened eyes. That evening someone silently brought you a new one – a little lopsided, shaped by hand.
ev.v_rage_home.text.5: Someone in the house was making noise at night and keeping you awake, and you had to be up before dawn. You leapt up and yelled at everyone so loudly the neighbours woke. Nobody in the house slept a wink till morning – out of fear, this time.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.5: In the morning the first thing you did was apologise – and admit you had frightened yourself in the night. That evening the house was noisy again, but with laughter.
ev.v_rage_home.text.6: Everything was ready for the feast when someone in the household oversalted the main dish. You swept it off the table onto the floor. The guests were greeted with a ruined supper and red eyes.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.6: You went out to the guests and apologised to the household in front of everyone. They ate flatbread and greens, and the feast turned out well after all.
ev.v_rage_home.text.7: At supper someone made a joke about your misfortune. You leapt up, knocked over the bench and said things you wouldn't say to an enemy. The joker went pale; the rest stared into their bowls.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.7: In the morning you took your words back – one by one, without hurrying. People joke more carefully around you now, but they've stopped being afraid.
ev.v_rage_home.text.8: You spent all morning searching for your best belt and decided someone in the household had taken it. You turned the whole house upside down, shouting and accusing everyone in sight. The household huddles in the corners.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.8: The belt turned up under your own bed. You showed it to everyone, spread your hands and apologised. They laughed at you – and that was the best thing that could have happened.
ev.v_rage_home.text.9: The roof had been leaking for three weeks, the debts were growing, and today someone knocked a bowl of water right onto your bed. That was the last straw: you tore the pot from its hook and hurled it into the corner.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.9: You sat down in the middle of the puddle and suddenly laughed. Everyone laughed after you. Then you apologised, and you patched the roof together.
ev.v_rage_home.text.10: You were arguing over whose turn it was to fetch firewood – and suddenly realised you were shouting, your fist already coming down on the table so hard a plank split. Everyone is looking at you as if seeing you for the first time.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.10: Without a word you picked up a rope and went for firewood yourself. When you came back, you asked forgiveness. The cracked plank was never replaced – now it serves as a reminder.
ev.v_rage_home.text.11: At the market you were short-changed and laughed at, and you carried your anger all the way home. There it spilled over – onto the first person in your way. You kicked a basket so hard the provisions rolled all over the floor.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.11: You picked the provisions up off the floor and admitted who you were really angry with. They understood – and even suggested what to say to that trader.
ev.v_rage_home.text.12: You came home late, hungry and angry, and supper had gone cold. You banged your bowl on the table so hard it split, and said everything that had built up over a year. The household listened in silence.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.12: You warmed up the leftovers yourself, shared them out among everyone and asked forgiveness. The cold supper turned into a warm conversation.
ev.v_rage_home.text.13: You tripped in the dark over things left lying in the yard and banged your knee. You burst into the house shouting so loudly that everyone jumped up, and swept everything off the table.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.13: Your knee was bandaged by the very people you'd been shouting at. You felt so ashamed that you apologised twice.
ev.v_rage_home.text.14: You were told the savings had been spent without asking you. You wouldn't hear any explanations: you tore a shelf from the wall and shouted until you were hoarse. The explanations went unspoken.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.14: Once you'd cooled down, you finally listened: the money had gone on medicine for the old man next door – the one you had once promised to help yourself. You asked forgiveness for a long time.
ev.v_rage_home.text.15: You woke with a splitting head, and of course everyone in the house was banging the dishes. You grabbed the nearest pot and smashed it on the floor: “Quiet!” It got very quiet.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.15: You swept up the shards and said a headache was no excuse. That evening someone quietly brought you a brew for the headache. The silence turned warm.
ev.v_rage_home.text.16: The household invited a guest you can't stand – without even asking you. In front of everyone you slammed a jug on the table and threw the guest out of the door. The household still won't meet your eyes.
ev.v_rage_home.apologize.ok.16: You went to the guest to apologise, and when you got back you asked forgiveness at home too. The guest, as it turned out, wasn't so bad after all.
ev.c_h_bone.text.1: You slipped on wet steps and heard a crack. The leg is swelling before your eyes, and you can't put any weight on it.
ev.c_h_bone.text.2: You climbed onto the roof to fix what the wind had torn loose and slid down along with a piece of the roofing. You landed badly: your leg is twisted, and the pain makes everything go dark.
ev.c_h_bone.text.3: A rung of the old ladder snapped under your foot, and then something in your leg snapped too. You're lying among scattered sacks, unable to get up.
ev.c_h_bone.text.4: On a mountain path the scree slid away under your feet, and you tumbled down with the stones. Your leg feels caught in a vice – it won't obey you and is swelling fast.
ev.c_h_bone.text.5: Coming home after dark, you put your foot into a hole someone had dug in the middle of the road and left uncovered. You heard the crack before the pain came.
ev.c_h_bone.text.6: On a dare you tried to jump a wide ditch – and fell short. Your leg folded on the edge with a dry snap, and now you can't put any weight on it.
ev.c_h_bone.text.7: Helping the neighbours raise a shed, you didn't jump clear in time when a log slipped. It struck your shin, and at once the leg felt like someone else's – heavy and hot.
ev.c_h_bone.text.8: At the festival you were dancing so well that everyone clapped – until you slipped on someone's spilled stew. The clapping stopped when it became clear you weren't getting up.
ev.c_h_bone.text.9: You climbed to the very top of the tree for the fruit, where it's ripest. The branch decided you were heavier than ripe fruit. Down below, hard ground and a sharp pain in your leg were waiting.
ev.c_h_bone.text.10: You were crossing the river on wet stones and slipped on the last one. Your foot jammed between two boulders while the rest of you kept falling. The pain is too much even to cry out.
ev.c_h_bone.text.11: In the holiday crush at the gate you were knocked off your feet, and someone heavy stepped right on your shin. They carried you out of the crowd – you could no longer walk on your own.
ev.c_h_bone.text.12: A stranger's dog lunged at you from a gateway; you took off running and went head over heels over a low fence. The dog gave up the chase. The pain in your leg didn't.
ev.c_h_bone.text.13: The rim of the old well collapsed while you were drawing water, and you slid down the slippery stonework. They hauled you out with a rope, but your leg hangs at an odd angle and it's frightening to look at.
ev.c_h_bone.text.14: After the downpour the clay path turned slick as ice. You took one step – and your feet went in different directions. You managed to draw one back; the other is still lying at the wrong angle.
ev.c_h_bone.text.15: A heavy sack of grain came crashing down on you from a tall stack. You'd have stayed on your feet if not for your leg: it buckled with a sickening crunch.
ev.c_h_bone.text.16: At night you were going down the dark stairs without a lamp and missed a step. Having counted all the rest on the way down, you ended up at the bottom – with a leg that won't hold you.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.1: {npc} dragged you into an eating house for "just one cup." It came to five, and the argument over whose neighborhood is better was never settled – even though you live on the same street.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.2: {npc} invited you to celebrate a lucky deal and naturally “forgot” {g=npc_sex:his|her} purse at home. You paid, but you heard about the deal three times – and each time it got luckier.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.3: {npc} talked you into stopping at the eating house by the gate, which rumour said served the best stew in town. The stew was so-so, but the conversation went on deep into the night.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.4: {npc} ran into you on the street and wouldn't let you go until you were both sitting at a table in the nearest eating house. You recalled old pranks and laughed so hard the owner twice asked you to keep it down.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.5: {npc} lost a bet to you and took you to an eating house to pay up. On the way it emerged that you'd be the one paying after all: “I've got nothing on me.”
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.6: After a long day {npc} dragged you into a noisy eating house where a street singer was performing. The singer was off-key, you both sang along even worse, and you came home with no voice but very happy.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.7: {npc} came round to complain about life, and you decided to do the complaining at an eating house. An hour later life seemed quite bearable, and two hours later you were planning to get rich on dried fish.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.8: On a feast day {npc} led you from one food stall to the next: “Try this, and this, and this one too.” By evening your purse was thinner – and you weren't.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.9: {npc} declared {g=npc_sex:he|she} knew a place that fed you better than the palace. The place turned out to be a cellar with three tables and one pot. But the food really was excellent, and the landlady sang.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.10: {npc} suggested waiting out the rain in an eating house. The rain soon stopped; the conversation didn't. You sat there until dark, sharing flatbread and other people's gossip.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.11: {npc} turned up with some news – whether good or bad was unclear – and you sorted it out at a table in an eating house. You decided it was good. To be safe, you celebrated twice.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.12: {npc} called you into an eating house “just for a moment” where people were playing dice. You didn't play, but you advised the players so loudly that the owner treated you on the house – one round. You paid for everything else.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.13: {npc} was marking the anniversary of a narrow escape and invited you along. Over the evening the tale of the escape gained a great many details. So did the bill.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.14: {npc} kept coaxing you to “just sit together like the old days.” So you did. Like the old days, you argued yourselves hoarse over which of you had been first up on that famous roof – and again couldn't agree.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.15: Toward evening {npc} knocked on your door with hot pies and a proposal to “add something to them at the eating house.” You did. The pies ran out first, the talk last.
ev.a_friend_tavern.text.16: {npc} saw you were gloomy and, without a word, led you to an eating house. {g=npc_sex:He|She} asked no questions, just kept your cup filled and told silly stories until you laughed.
ev.f_religious_school.text.1: The teacher at the temple offers to teach you to read and to study the holy books. That means hours over letters instead of games and chores.
ev.f_religious_school.text.1.chinese_fol: The village teacher offers to teach you characters and the classics of the sages. That means hours over a brush instead of games and chores.
ev.f_religious_school.text.1.christian: The monks at the monastery teach children to read from the Psalter. They are willing to take you – hours over letters instead of games and chores.
ev.f_religious_school.text.1.islamic: The teacher at the mosque offers to take you into the maktab: reading, writing and learning the Quran by heart. That means hours over a slate instead of games and chores.
ev.f_religious_school.text.1.jewish: The community's teacher offers to teach you to read the Torah. That means hours over letters instead of games and chores.
ev.f_religious_school.text.2: The old man who copies the holy texts noticed you peering at the letters over his shoulder and offered to teach you. It would mean sitting over the writing every morning while the other children run about by the river.
ev.f_religious_school.text.3: The teacher at the house of prayer heard how clearly you repeat the prayers and is inviting you to study: reading, writing and learning the holy books by heart. They say he has a heavy hand and a kind heart.
ev.f_religious_school.text.4: At the holy place they gather children in the mornings, and whoever reads best gets to sit right by the wall, where it's warm. They're offering you a place – by the entrance for now, in the draught. To move to the wall you'll have to toil over the writing.
ev.f_religious_school.text.5: A man of the faith came into your yard himself and said you had a good head that it would be a pity to spend on chores alone. He'll teach you the holy books – if you're ready to get up before dawn.
ev.f_religious_school.text.6: The scribe at the shrine is looking for an apprentice to help copy prayers, and in return he'll teach reading and writing. The work is dull and your fingers will be forever inky, but you'll be able to read what few people can.
ev.f_religious_school.text.7: You were scratching squiggles in the sand with a stick when a passing teacher stopped and said one of them was a real letter. Now he's inviting you to study properly: to write, to read and to make sense of the holy texts.
ev.f_religious_school.text.8: Every morning under the big tree by the shrine, a teacher gathers children, reads them the holy books and makes them repeat. You're invited too. The ones who go can already write their own names and are terribly proud of it.
ev.f_religious_school.text.9: The keeper of the house of prayer teaches children in the evenings, once the work is done. The light of an oil lamp, a quiet voice, sacred words – and endless letters to copy until they come out straight.
ev.f_religious_school.text.10: The teacher at the holy place promises that whoever learns the sacred texts will be able to read a letter, reckon debts and argue with the headman himself. Lessons every day except feast days.
ev.f_religious_school.text.11: The children from the neighbouring yards have been going to the teacher at the shrine for a month and now they're putting on airs: they know whole prayers by heart and can write. The teacher has sent word that he'll take you too.
ev.f_religious_school.text.12: They say of the teacher at the house of prayer: strict to the point of terror, and a blot means no lunch. But his pupils read the holy books so well that the grown-ups stop to listen. He's willing to take you.
ev.f_religious_school.text.13: At the festival you saw a boy hardly older than you read a sacred text before everyone while the grown-ups listened with bated breath. His teacher says you could do it too – after three years of hard work.
ev.f_religious_school.text.14: A wandering man of learning has settled in the district for a while. In return for board and lodging he teaches children to read and the holy books, and every morning his house is crowded with pupils. There's room for you as well.
ev.f_religious_school.text.15: You learned a prayer by ear faster than anyone in your yard, and the teacher at the shrine heard about it. He thinks it's time you studied properly: from the written word, not just by memory.
ev.f_religious_school.text.16: The teacher at the holy place handed you a smooth board and a lump of charcoal: “Come tomorrow at dawn – we'll begin.” You'd start with the first letter. You'd finish many years from now, when you can read the holy books yourself.
ev.a_boundary.text.1: Over the winter the boundary stone between your field and your neighbor's has "walked" about ten paces. For some reason it never walks in your direction.
ev.a_boundary.text.1.egypt: After the flood the field boundaries always wash away, and the surveyors measure out the plots again. But your neighbor got there first, and his field is suddenly a good ten paces wider.
ev.a_boundary.text.1.rome: Over the winter the boundary stone between your field and your neighbor's has "walked" about ten paces – and such stones are sacred to the god Terminus. For some reason it never walks in your direction.
ev.a_boundary.text.2: In spring you found that the boundary stone by the stream now stands on this side of the old tree instead of that one. The tree hasn't moved. So someone else has.
ev.a_boundary.text.3: Around the boundary stone the earth is freshly dug, and the stone itself stands a good strip closer to your house. Your neighbour insists it “has always been here” – while looking somewhere off to the side.
ev.a_boundary.text.4: The new neighbour had barely moved in when he walked the boundary first thing – and the boundary stone somehow slid eight paces your way. “That's how it was under the previous owner,” he says. The previous owner would have disagreed.
ev.a_boundary.text.5: Your neighbour sowed right up to the stone and then, it seems, couldn't stop: his shoots are already coming up on your land, and the boundary stone has been dragged into the bushes as if it belonged there.
ev.a_boundary.text.6: In the night you heard scuffling and puffing by the boundary, and in the morning the boundary stone turned up in a new spot – along with a trail of fresh footprints to your neighbour's yard. The neighbour looked very tired that morning.
ev.a_boundary.text.7: After heavy rains the boundary stone “slid” onto your land. Your neighbour says the water did it. Strange, though, that the water dragged a heavy stone uphill.
ev.a_boundary.text.8: The boundary stone between you and the old man next door has moved ten paces onto your side. The old man swears he couldn't even lift it himself – but he has three strapping hired hands and very honest eyes.
ev.a_boundary.text.9: Right before the harvest you noticed the boundary stone standing in the middle of your crops rather than at their edge. Your neighbour is already sharpening his sickle and seems set on reaping right up to the stone.
ev.a_boundary.text.10: The boundary stone had borne a carved mark since olden times – but now the mark is gone: the stone has been turned over and shifted ten paces your way. Your neighbour spreads his hands: “The earth moves by itself.”
ev.a_boundary.text.11: A shepherd boy whispered to you that at dawn he saw your neighbour rolling the boundary stone along with a pole. The stone is indeed on your land now. The boy asked for a flatbread for his trouble – and for you not to tell anyone where you heard it.
ev.a_boundary.text.12: The boundary stone has moved only a couple of paces – you wouldn't have noticed if you didn't pace out the boundary every spring. This year there are fewer paces. The neighbour, it seems, has decided to nibble away a little at a time.
ev.a_boundary.text.13: The boundary stone has vanished altogether. You found it in the gully, and where it used to stand your neighbour has already driven in pegs – on your side, naturally.
ev.a_boundary.text.14: Your neighbour met you by the boundary stone, patted it like an old friend and announced that it stands “where it should.” Only a year ago this old friend stood by the dry bush, and the bush hasn't gone anywhere.
ev.a_boundary.text.15: The old neighbour died, and his heir has taken over with great energy: first thing, the boundary stone moved twelve paces onto your land. “Grandad always said this was our land,” he explains.
ev.a_boundary.text.16: While the whole village was out at the festival, the boundary stone quietly moved over to your side. Your neighbour never showed up at the festival – said his back was hurting. His back, it seems, got better by morning.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.1: {npc} walked past you in the market in a new cloak and pretended not to see you. You pretended too – but, it seems, less convincingly.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.2: {npc} was loudly boasting in the square about a fine bargain, and, of course, everyone was listening. You walked past looking like someone who didn't care – and tripped over your own foot.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.3: At the feast {npc} sat in a place of honour, while you were seated at the far end beside a half-deaf old man. All evening the old man kept asking who that important person was.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.4: You found out that {npc} had bought the very house you'd been saving for for three years. By evening {g=npc_sex:he|she} was already sitting at its gate, waving at you cheerfully.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.5: {npc} walked past with a crowd of friends and laughed loudly – maybe not at you. But you spent the whole day wondering at what.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.6: At the well {npc} casually mentioned that things couldn't be going better. You said the same was true for you – and regretted not coming up with something more convincing.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.7: {npc} was sitting in an eating house surrounded by your old acquaintances, all of them hanging on {g=npc_sex:his|her} every word. They nodded to you – and turned back to {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.8: {npc} strolled down the street with a new servant carrying {g=npc_sex:his|her} purchases. At that very moment you were lugging your own and nearly dropped them out of sheer annoyance.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.9: You overheard {npc} saying to someone about you, “Oh, that one…” The rest was lost in the noise, which was probably for the best. Though your imagination filled it all in anyway.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.10: {npc} haggled at the same stall as you and got half the price. The trader even smiled. He has never smiled at you.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.11: {npc} lingered nearby on purpose so you could get a good look at {g=npc_sex:his|her} new embroidered belt. You did. Afterwards you quietly pulled your old belt tighter, as if that would make it newer.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.12: At the gathering {npc} spoke so smoothly that everyone nodded approvingly. You meant to say something too, but by the time you'd found the words everyone had gone home.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.13: {npc} greeted you politely in front of everyone – so politely that it was clear to all who stood higher. You returned the greeting, but it came out rather sour.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.14: A neighbour told you {npc} was on the rise again: new connections, new ventures. You said, “Good for them,” – and then spent half the day angry at that neighbour.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.15: In a narrow alley {npc} came toward you, and neither of you wanted to give way. You did – into a puddle. {npc} didn't even look back.
ev.a_rival_seen.text.16: {npc} was handing out treats at the gate to celebrate some stroke of luck and offered you a flatbread too – with such a gracious smile that it stuck in your throat.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.1: You held your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} for the first time – and {npc} promptly grabbed your nose and wouldn't let go. The parents say {g=npc_sex:he|she} takes after you.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.2: {npc} was so tiny you were afraid to breathe. But the moment you took your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} in your arms, {g=npc_sex:he|she} stopped crying and gave you a very serious stare.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.3: They put your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} in your arms right on the doorstep before you'd even shaken off the dust of the road. {npc} sneezed in your face – and everyone decided it was a good omen.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.4: You held your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} clumsily, as if for the first time, though you'd once raised children of your own. {npc} didn't mind: {g=npc_sex:he|she} yawned and fell asleep on your shoulder.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.5: {npc} gripped your finger tight and didn't let go until {g=npc_sex:he|she} fell asleep. You sat without moving until evening – and never once regretted it.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.6: You had barely picked up your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} when {npc} cheerfully soaked your best clothes. The parents were mortified, but you laughed harder than you had in years.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.7: Everyone was arguing over whom {npc} took after. You picked {g=npc_sex:him|her} up and knew at once: you. That nose is definitely yours.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.8: You sang your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} the same lullaby that was once sung to you – and were surprised to find you remembered every word. {npc} listened open-mouthed and fell asleep on the last verse.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.9: They sat you in the place of honour and carefully laid a bundle in your lap. Out of the bundle {npc} peered up at you – wrinkled, red, and the most beautiful person in the world.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.10: {npc} was howling so loud that neither the parents nor the neighbour women could settle {g=npc_sex:him|her}. They handed {g=npc_sex:him|her} to you “for a moment” – and the crying stopped at once. Since then you get called every time there are tears.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.11: You came a long way to hold your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} for the first time. {npc} studied your face long and carefully, then suddenly smiled. For that smile it would have been worth walking twice as far.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.12: Holding your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, you suddenly felt very old – and very happy. {npc} snuffled quietly, blowing bubbles, and seemed equally pleased with everything.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.13: They let you hold your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} while the parents ate. {npc} immediately grabbed your ear and pulled so hard that everyone could tell {g=npc_sex:he|she}'d grow up strong.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.14: In your arms {npc} opened {g=npc_sex:his|her} eyes for a long while for the first time and looked straight at you. The parents insist babies that small can't see anything yet. You know they're wrong.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.15: {npc} lay in your arms so warm and heavy that you didn't want to give {g=npc_sex:him|her} back. The parents coughed politely, but you pretended not to hear.
ev.c_grand_first_hold.text.16: You were afraid your arms weren't what they used to be, but {npc} settled into them as snugly as if {g=npc_sex:he|she}'d always lived there. The neighbours said afterwards they'd never seen you so content.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.1: Late one evening you happen to see the steward carrying out sacks of the master's grain and rewriting the accounts. He looks up – and realizes you saw everything. “Surely we can come to an arrangement,” he says quietly.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.2: You've noticed the steward keeps two sets of scales: one for the master, one for buyers. The difference ends up in his chest. Yesterday he caught your eye and smiled: “Sharp eyes you have. That could turn out to be profitable.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master weighed the goods on both scales himself and his face darkened. The steward was driven out in disgrace, and now the master watches you closely – with interest, it seems.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.3: At night by the back gate the steward was handing bales of the master's cloth to some strangers. You were standing in the shadows, but he turned round anyway. “Can't sleep?” he asked. “Let's talk like sensible people.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master counted the bales in the storeroom and came up twenty short. The steward was led away under guard, and the master called you in and questioned you at length – and not only about the theft.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.4: You happened to see the steward topping up the master's oil jars with water and carrying the surplus oil off to his own place. He spotted you and wasn't even embarrassed: “There's enough here for everyone. You too.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master had one jar poured out – and the oil and water separated into layers in front of everyone. The steward was sold that same month, and the master thanked you for the first time – and seems to have remembered you.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.5: Every spring some of the master's young animals “die,” and the steward notes it down carefully. Yet yesterday you saw those “dead” animals alive and well – at the market in the next settlement, next to his man. The steward saw you too. “Shall we talk?” he whispered that evening.
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master sent people to the neighbouring market, and there they found his animals with his own marks on them. The steward was driven out in disgrace, and the master called you the only honest person in the house.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.6: The steward dropped his bunch of keys and you handed it back – noticing there was one key more than there should be: to the master's strongroom of valuables. He took the keys and said very gently: “You didn't see anything, did you? And if you did – let's come to an arrangement.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master checked the strongroom and found half his valuables missing. The key was found tucked in the steward's belt. The thief was bound and taken away, and the master brought you closer to him.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.7: You found out the steward collects pay from the master for workers who are long gone: some dead, some moved away. Their share ends up with him. Yesterday he realised you knew and took you aside: “Shall we talk?”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master had all the workers assembled and called out their names. Barely half answered. The steward was driven out, and the master remembered you – for a long time, it seems.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.8: Mending the granary wall, you found a hiding place behind a loose stone: the master's valuables tied up in a rag. That same evening the steward came to you himself: “I hear you've been mending the wall. Let's come to an arrangement while nobody knows anything.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master pulled out the stone himself and stared at the rag for a long time. The steward was thrown out the same day, and the master told you to come straight to him – if you notice anything else.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.9: During the milling you noticed the steward scooping a handful from every one of the master's sacks into his own. A handful isn't much. But there are hundreds of sacks. He caught you by the sleeve: “You're clever. Why should we quarrel?”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master had the sacks reweighed and saw the shortfall at once. The thief was sent to the hardest labour, and for the first time the master trusted you with the storeroom key.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.10: At dusk you saw the steward selling the master's tools to a travelling trader – at half price, but without prying eyes. As it turned out, there were prying eyes after all. “Quiet,” he told you when the trader had gone. “There's a share for you too.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master tracked the trader down at the market, and the trader, wanting no trouble, told him everything. The steward was thrown out, and the master praised you in front of everyone – for the first time you can remember.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.11: You noticed the steward shaving notches off the tally sticks when no one was looking – and every time, part of the master's harvest vanished. He shaved the last notch right in front of you. “Well then,” he sighed. “Now we'll have to come to an arrangement.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master checked the sticks against his own memory and found the shavings. The steward was driven out, and the master made you keeper of the tally sticks – who knows, maybe that's only the beginning.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.12: In the night an empty granary caught fire, and the steward loudly mourned the “burned grain.” Only you had seen that grain being carried out of the yard the day before. In the morning he found you himself: “Whatever you saw – forget it. And I won't forget to show my gratitude.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master had the ashes raked through – and found not a single grain. The steward was taken away, and the master remembered you so well that the household is already whispering.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.13: You saw the steward swapping good cloth in the master's bales for rotten stuff and stashing the good cloth at his own place. He didn't even bother denying it: “Want a length? Take it. Just hold your tongue.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master slit open a couple of bales and found the rot. The steward was thrown out in disgrace, and the master gave you a length of that very good cloth – with a look as if he had something in mind.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.14: At the market you recognised the buyer as the agent of a neighbouring household – and realised the grain he was taking away had been in your master's storeroom only yesterday. Beside him stood the steward, counting the takings. He looked up and smiled with his lips only: “Shall we discuss it tonight?”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master counted the sacks – and went pale. The neighbour's agent confessed everything, the steward was driven out, and the master began calling you by name. Before, he didn't seem to know it.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.15: Precious jewellery has gone missing from the mistress's chest, and they're already hunting for a culprit among the servants. But you saw the steward leaving her rooms with a bundle. He knows you saw: “Keep quiet – and I'll make sure suspicion falls on someone other than you.”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master had the steward's room searched, and the bundle was found under a floorboard. The thief was taken away, and the master called you an honest person in front of everyone – something rarely heard here.
ev.t_uncover_crime.text.16: The master allots plenty of food for the workers, yet the common pot holds little but water. You tracked down where the rest goes: the steward sells the grain on the side. Catching you by his hiding place, he sighed: “So – are we going to quarrel, or share?”
ev.t_uncover_crime.report_master.success: The master came to the common pot himself, tasted the stew and understood everything. The steward was driven out, the workers were finally fed properly, and the master took notice of you – perhaps more than you think.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.1: In the night your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} is burning with fever and won't feed. So small a child, so great a fever. By morning you must decide where to run for help.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.2: {npc} fussed all evening, and by night had grown hot as a sun-baked stone and gone quiet. The quiet is more frightening than crying. You must decide whom to send for.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.3: The neighbours are still finishing the festival songs, while {npc} tosses in the cradle with burning cheeks, crying without a voice. The guests have gone, the healer is probably asleep. But waiting until morning is frightening.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.4: At first you thought it was teething: {npc} chewed on everything and whimpered. But by night the fever came, and the baby won't feed any more. This isn't teething.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.5: The night is stifling, and {npc} is burning hotter than the air. You keep laying your palm on the baby's forehead – and snatching it back every time. Morning seems very far away.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.6: A children's fever is going round the street, and now it has reached your cradle. {npc} is breathing fast and shallow, cheeks burning. The neighbour woman whispers one thing, the healer says another – and you must decide before dawn.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.7: You stopped for the night in a strange village, and in the middle of the night {npc} woke burning with fever. You know no one here – no healer, no herb-woman, no holy place. You'll have to ask your hosts.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.8: Rain is pouring outside, the roof leaks in the corner, and {npc} is burning up and crying hoarsely. To fetch help you'll have to run through the downpour across half the village. Run you must – the only question is where.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.9: You woke in the night to a strange silence. {npc} isn't crying, just moaning softly, and {g=npc_sex:his|her} forehead is hot as a hearthstone. You can't wait until morning.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.10: A red rash has spread over your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc}'s body, and by evening a fever set in. The old women shake their heads, each with her own advice. It's for you to decide – and quickly.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.11: {npc} loved being bathed in the river so much, but by night the fever began. Now {g=npc_sex:he|she} won't feed and just looks at you with clouded eyes.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.12: For the third night {npc} has been crying without stopping, and tonight a fever has joined the crying. You can't remember when you last slept. But sleep will have to wait: you must decide where to run.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.13: The baby's forehead is hot and the little feet icy cold – the old women say that's the worst sign. {npc} is breathing heavily. Help must be found before dawn.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.14: Everyone in the house is asleep; only you sit by the cradle. {npc} tosses in fever and doesn't recognise you. You're alone with this night and this decision.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.15: The night turned cold and you wrapped the baby up warmly, but {npc} is burning from the inside regardless. The fire in the hearth has nearly died, while the child's fever keeps climbing.
ev.c_infant_fever.text.16: Until now {npc} hadn't been ill a single day, and you'd even boasted about it to the neighbours. Tonight the baby is burning and won't open {g=npc_sex:his|her} eyes. You don't feel like boasting any more – you just want dawn to come.
ev.c_h_cough.text.1: The cough has hung on since winter and has no intention of leaving: at night your chest feels stuffed with wool. The physician shakes his head and advises what he advises all wealthy patients – a long journey and dry air.
ev.c_h_cough.text.2: The walls of the house are forever damp, and the cough has moved into your chest along with the damp. The healer is blunt: as long as you breathe this mould, you won't get better. Go away for a while somewhere dry and sunny – if you can afford it.
ev.c_h_cough.text.3: Days are bearable, but at night the cough keeps you and the whole household awake. The physician listened to your chest, frowned and said: “Honey and rest are for the poor. You ought to go somewhere dry for a month or two.”
ev.c_h_cough.text.4: You caught a chill back in the wet season, and the cough has never left. Your neighbour advises a trip somewhere the air is hot and dry: it saved an acquaintance of his, he says. Meanwhile the physician takes his fee every day and spreads his hands.
ev.c_h_cough.text.5: Every morning begins with a long fit of coughing that makes your vision go dark. The old physician advises what his own teacher once advised: a warm dry land, sunshine and no fogs. The journey isn't cheap. Neither is coughing.
ev.c_h_cough.text.6: Your chest wheezes like old bellows, and climbing stairs has become torture. The physician said the damp will be the end of you and advised going away to warm, dry lands for a while.
ev.c_h_cough.text.7: A passing traveller, hearing your cough, told of lands where the sun blazes all year and the air is so dry wounds heal twice as fast. “A cough like that is gone in a month there,” he assured you. At home this one has hung on for half a year.
ev.c_h_cough.text.8: Every morning fog lies over the river, and your cough only grows stronger from it. The physician put it bluntly: go far from the water, somewhere dry – or prepare to cough for the rest of your days.
ev.c_h_cough.text.9: You've tried everything: brews, hot stones, herbs and charms. The cough only snickers. The last physician you called in said only the dry air of distant lands could help.
ev.c_h_cough.text.10: The cough has eaten your voice: now you speak hoarsely and quietly, and you're afraid to laugh – it sets off a fit at once. The physician advises going to warm dry lands before your chest weakens for good.
ev.c_h_cough.text.11: The year turned out cold and wet, and the cough has clung to you like a burr. The neighbours now recognise you by it from a distance. People who know about these things advise going away for a while to where there's sun and a dry wind.
ev.c_h_cough.text.12: The cough has left you so weak that work slips from your hands, and after every fit you have to sit down. The physician keeps repeating himself: dry air, sunshine, a journey. Everything else, he says, is a waste of money.
ev.c_h_cough.text.13: The smoke from the hearth stings your eyes, and the cough eats at your chest. For months now you haven't been able to catch your breath. The healer says: “You won't recover at home. Go somewhere the air is dry and clean, even for a little while.”
ev.c_h_cough.text.14: You haven't got out of bed for a week – the cough takes all your strength. The household brings you hot drinks, and the physician, standing by the bed, advises what he says helps best of all: a long journey to warm, dry lands.
ev.c_h_cough.text.15: Spring has come and everything around you is coming back to life, while you cough as if it were the dampest season. The physician says the illness has settled deep and only hot dry air can drive it out – somewhere far from here.
ev.c_h_cough.text.16: A trader you know listened to you cough and offered you a place with his party heading for hot, dry lands: “A month under that sun and you'll forget what a cough is.” The place isn't free, mind you. Meanwhile the cough has hung on since autumn.
ev.c_far_away.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} wants to leave: {g=npc_sex:sign on with merchants or the army and see the world|go with her husband to a distant land where his family has a business}. Promises to come back rich. You recall that everyone promises that.
ev.c_far_away.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has decided to seek {g=npc_sex:his|her} fortune in the capital: {g=npc_sex:they say strong hands and sharp minds are wanted there|they say wealthy houses there are looking for skilled needlewomen}. The bundle is already packed; only your word is missing.
ev.c_far_away.text.3: {npc} has heard of a famous master in a distant city who takes apprentices, and has talked of nothing else since. The road is long, and the training longer still. But {g=npc_sex:his|her} eyes are shining so brightly that it's hard to argue.
ev.c_far_away.text.4: {npc} has made friends with the merchants who were lodging with you, and they're inviting {g=npc_sex:him|her} along: carrying, counting, trading. In a year, they promise, {g=npc_sex:he|she}'ll be leading a train of {g=npc_sex:his|her} own.
ev.c_far_away.text.5: {npc} is set on going over the mountains, where, rumour has it, the land yields twice as much and there's room for everyone. “Once I'm settled, I'll send for you all,” {g=npc_sex:he|she} says. You've heard that before.
ev.c_far_away.text.6: A learned man has noticed how quickly {npc} picks everything up, and is inviting {g=npc_sex:him|her} to a distant city to study with the wise. {g=npc_sex:He|She}'ll come back someone people listen to, he says. If {g=npc_sex:he|she} comes back.
ev.c_far_away.text.7: {npc} has vowed to walk to a distant holy place and is now preparing for a journey that will take more than a year. “I'll come back a different person,” {g=npc_sex:he|she} says. You fear that “different” doesn't mean “the same.”
ev.c_far_away.text.8: {npc} caught the eye of a noble guest from the capital, who is inviting {g=npc_sex:him|her} into his service. The post is honourable and far away – so far that news will take months to arrive.
ev.c_far_away.text.9: Since childhood {npc} has gazed down the road, and now {g=npc_sex:he|she} has announced {g=npc_sex:he|she}'s leaving – where to, {g=npc_sex:he|she} doesn't know yet, just to see what lies beyond the edge of things. “I'll come back with stories,” {g=npc_sex:he|she} smiles.
ev.c_far_away.text.10: Word has spread through the district that across the river empty land is being given to anyone willing to work it. {npc} has already arranged to go with friends. “I'll have a household of my own,” {g=npc_sex:he|she} says. “I can't live under your roof forever.”
ev.c_far_away.text.11: Workers are being hired for a great building project in a distant city, and they say the pay is generous. {npc} has already given {g=npc_sex:his|her} word and is only waiting for your blessing. The building will take years.
ev.c_far_away.text.12: {npc} has had word from an old friend who has settled in a distant city and is calling {g=npc_sex:him|her} to come: there's work, there's lodging, all that's missing is someone to trust. {npc} is already looking down the road.
ev.c_far_away.text.13: “I feel cramped here,” {npc} said at supper, setting down {g=npc_sex:his|her} spoon. {g=npc_sex:He|She} wants to go to a big city where no one knows {g=npc_sex:him|her} or your family, and start everything {g=npc_sex:his|her} own way.
ev.c_far_away.text.14: You quarrelled again, and this time {npc} didn't slam the door but said calmly: “I'm leaving. Far away. I'll live by my own wits.” The bundle, it seems, had been packed in advance.
ev.c_far_away.text.15: {npc} has heard plenty of tales about people who left poor and came back with chests full, and now is eager to follow. “I'm no worse than they were,” {g=npc_sex:he|she} says. That's true. But luck doesn't ask who's worse.
ev.c_far_away.text.16: At dawn you saw {npc} sitting on the doorstep with a walking staff. {g=npc_sex:He|She} decided long ago to go off to distant lands and was only waiting to tell you face to face.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.1: The goat had twins, and the weakest kid was given to you to raise. Now it follows you everywhere and chews the hem of your shirt.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.2: The kid was born in the night, and in the morning you were the first to find it. The grown-ups decided: you found it, you raise it. Now every morning it butts you instead of saying hello.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.3: A little kid strayed from the herd, and you were the one who brought it back. Ever since it's been considered yours: you bring it the best grass, and it leaps all over you as if you were a rock.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.4: The lamb was born weak, and you were told to feed it from a horn. A month later it's strong and follows you everywhere, bleating pitifully the moment you step away.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.5: The kid you nursed all spring has learned to jump onto the shed roof. The grown-ups grumble, but you're secretly proud: after all, you raised it.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.6: You were trusted with a brood of ducklings. You led them to the stream, counted them ten times a day and didn't lose a single one. The ducklings seem convinced you're a big duck.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.7: The kid was born with a crooked leg, and they wanted to give it away to the neighbours. You begged to keep it, made it a splint from sticks – and it got better. Now it runs faster than any of them.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.8: The kid was given the name you chose – exactly the same as the village headman's. The grown-ups laugh, the kid answers to its name, and the headman, luckily, doesn't know yet.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.9: The calf born in the cold season was freezing in the byre, so you hauled it armfuls of hay and sat beside it, warming its sides. Now it has doubled in size and still tries to snuggle up to you for warmth.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.10: Your kid ate half the neighbour's vegetable patch, and you had to apologise for it as if you'd done it yourself. But when it fell asleep that evening with its head on your knees, you forgave it everything.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.11: You were given some chicks that had hatched with no hen to mind them. You kept them in a basket by the hearth, fed them soaked grain – and now a cheeping yellow flock runs after you round the yard.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.12: The old nanny goat had twins, and you raised one of the kids almost single-handed. Now whenever you call, both come running – the second has evidently decided not to be left out.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.13: You were teaching your kid to walk on a rope like a dog. It learned – but it only goes where it wants. You follow it, and that suits you both.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.14: The gosling you pulled out of a ditch has grown into a bad-tempered goose. It nips everyone in sight – except you. You it escorts to the well and back like a guard.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.15: The kid got bored of its pen and ran off. You spent half the day searching the whole neighbourhood and found it on the roof of someone else's shed. The grown-ups roared with laughter, and you carried the runaway home in your arms like a hero.
ev.y_goat_kid.text.16: You were allowed to choose a kid from the new litter yourself. You picked the smallest, shaggiest one, though everyone advised another. Now it's grown, and everyone admits you chose well.
ev.a_voyage.text.1: A captain you know is taking passengers with goods on a long voyage. Those who come back will sell at three times the price. Those who don't won't care either way.
ev.a_voyage.text.1.athens: A captain you know is sailing to the Black Sea for grain and salted fish, taking passengers with goods. Those who come back will sell at three times the price. Those who don't won't care either way.
ev.a_voyage.text.1.egypt: A caravan is heading for the Red Sea ports, where ships leave for incense and spices. Those who come back will sell at three times the price. Those who don't won't care either way.
ev.a_voyage.text.1.rome: A captain you know is sailing to Massalia and on to the coasts of Spain, taking passengers with goods. Those who come back will sell at three times the price. Those who don't won't care either way.
ev.a_voyage.text.2: The skipper of a big boat is heading downriver all the way to the mouth, where goods fetch three times the price, and he's looking for passengers with cargo. It's a long trip: rapids, shoals and rough folk on the banks. But the profit would last a whole year.
ev.a_voyage.text.3: A captain you know is making the last voyage before the stormy season and taking passengers with goods. The sea won't wait for latecomers, but those who make it will find empty markets and high prices.
ev.a_voyage.text.4: Down at the harbour they say that on foreign shores goods like yours sell for three times the price. A captain you know is willing to take you and your cargo. He's been there twice and come back both times – though the second time without half his crew.
ev.a_voyage.text.5: A captain you've dealt with many times makes an offer: take your goods out, sell them, use the takings to buy goods there – and sell those here. Two profits for one voyage. Provided, of course, it's one voyage and not the last.
ev.a_voyage.text.6: A young skipper has built a new vessel and is looking for his first passengers with cargo. The boat smells of fresh timber and pitch, the skipper of confidence. He has less experience than confidence, mind you.
ev.a_voyage.text.7: Far along the coast a great fair gathers once a year, where merchants from every land meet. A captain you know is sailing there and invites you along. Whoever brings goods first will skim the cream.
ev.a_voyage.text.8: Sailors say a distant port is short of exactly what you have, and prices there have soared. A captain is ready to cast off in three days. Rumours, though, are sometimes older than the ships that carry them.
ev.a_voyage.text.9: The wind has finally turned, and everyone in the harbour is in a hurry: the ships are leaving one after another. A skipper you know shouts from the deck that there's still room for your cargo – but you have to decide by sunset.
ev.a_voyage.text.10: An old captain with forty years at sea says this voyage will be his last, and he wants to go out in style: a full hold and reliable passengers. He considers you reliable. If only you knew how reliable he is himself.
ev.a_voyage.text.11: A captain is sailing to distant islands where, rumour has it, ordinary goods from the mainland fetch three times their worth. Nearly a month's sailing with no shore along the way. He's been looking for passengers with goods for a week – few are willing.
ev.a_voyage.text.12: A skipper is gathering boats to go up the great river to distant towns where goods arrive seldom and dear. Going against the current is hard, and the banks are unsettled. But upriver your cargo will fetch three times as much.
ev.a_voyage.text.13: Several traders have pooled their money to hire a ship for a long voyage and are inviting you to take a share: your cargo, your profit. The captain is experienced, the ship sturdy. Only the sea doesn't know that.
ev.a_voyage.text.14: After a long lull the harbour is bustling again: ships are getting ready for the first long voyages. A captain you know says the first always sell dearest. The first are also the ones caught in the last storms.
ev.a_voyage.title.15: A Word Given in the Tavern
ev.a_voyage.text.15: In a harbour eating house a tipsy captain held forth on the profits waiting on a distant shore and offered you room for your cargo. In the morning, sober, he confirmed the offer – so he meant it.
ev.a_voyage.text.16: They say this ship is lucky: five voyages, five profits. The captain is taking passengers with goods on the sixth. You know luck likes a count, but you don't know how high it can count.
